newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top Germans see hope for Thyssen-Krupp steel deal.
newsitem.headline: Top Germans see hope for Thyssen-Krupp steel deal.

text.p: Two leading German officials said on Sunday they expected talks between steelmakers Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp and Thyssen AG to avoid a hostile bid by Krupp would end in mutual cooperation.

Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the BDI Federation of German Industry, and Wolfgang Clement, economics minister of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, both said they were optimistic about the outcome of the ongoing talks ahead of a Thursday deadline.

"I would say a merger would be good for both companies, particularly in the long-term," Henkel told German television network ZDPF in an interview programme along with Clement, whose state is headquarters for both companies.
Clement, a member of the Social Democratic Party (SPD), said he had the "impression that these talks have been very constructive".
"I do not think the differences are dramatic. I want to see a merger in the end and not a hostile takeover," he said.
Henkel also said in the television programme that he believed the talks were "progressing well" based on his conversations with those involved in the talks.
"I am convinced that if nothing is done the situation will become much worse," Henkel said.
Added Clement: "We must come to a rational decision."

The talks began last Thursdy after Krupp launched a rare hostile takeover of larger Thyssen earlier last week, offering shareholders 435 marks a share, a 25 percent premium over the previous day's share price.
Krupp has set Thursday as a deadline for the talks amid German media reports at the weekend that it would relaunch its hostile takeover bid for Thyssen should the talks fail.

A merger between Krupp and Thyssen would create one of the world's largest steel operations, but Krupp has said the full merger of the two companies would create cost savings in other areas as well, such as engineering and automotive components.

The takeover attempt sparked spontaneous work stoppages by thousands of steel workers in the Ruhr valley heartland and local politicians intervened, persuading the two companies to begin talks over a merger of just their steel companies.
